One set of expectations in shared spaces—clean up after yourself, keep noise reasonable, be safe around kids, and treat people with basic respect. If we stick to those basics, most differences don’t turn into problems.

On tough stuff like alcoholism or substance use, I lean toward firm kindness. The garden and common areas should be safe and calm—no intoxication in the space, no paraphernalia left where kids could find it. If someone’s struggling, we offer a hand—point to local support, check in if they look unwell—but we don’t enable, and we don’t let safety slide. With infectious diseases, I think privacy and good hygiene come first. We don’t pry into people’s health or spread rumors. We keep shared tools clean, have handwashing stations at events, and follow public health guidance if something specific comes up. If someone asks for a bit more space or a small change to feel safe, we try to accommodate without making them feel singled out. Respect goes a long way.

Different racial, religious, and language backgrounds—this is where patience and curiosity help. Learn names, ask once more if you missed it, and don’t be shy about using a translation app or pointing to a sign. Post the garden rules in plain language, maybe with pictures. If someone’s observant of certain customs, we respect that—no big speeches, just everyday courtesy. Shared work builds bridges faster than any lecture.

Sexual orientation or how folks structure their family—honestly, that’s their business. Hold everyone to the same neighbor standards and keep moral judging out of it. responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character06_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:

If the company posts the overtime list, they follow it—no sliding a buddy to the top. He’d say help should be a hand up, not a lifetime pass. Folks who fall on hard times deserve a fair shake, but effort matters. What really rubbed him raw was when decisions felt rigged—by money, by connections, or by people far away who never had to live with the results.

Belonging, to him, was earned by showing up. You belong when you learn your neighbors’ names, shovel the sidewalk for the widow on the corner, and respect how the block does things. It wasn’t about where you came from—he meant that. It was about how you carry yourself. He’d tell the story of a new family on our street: didn’t say much at first, then one winter they were out at 6 a.m. helping dig cars out. After that, they were “ours.” That’s belonging—shared sweat, shared jokes, shared coffee in the cold.

Community was the safety net we built for ourselves: church-basement fish fries, passing the hat when someone’s furnace died, the union hall spaghetti dinners to cover a chemo bill. You handle small problems face to face before you call City Hall. You watch each other’s kids, you check on folks after a storm. He believed in second chances, but also in accountability—you break something, you fix it; you say you’ll show up, you show up. He wanted dignity for everybody, and he thought dignity comes from being needed and from pulling your weight.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character06_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
J: Sitting there with dirt under my nails and a thermos on the bench, I mostly feel curious and open. I like seeing different faces and hearing different accents drift across the beds. You can tell a lot about folks by how they treat a shared space—do they put the hose back, close the gate, pull a few weeds that aren’t “theirs.” That’s the language I speak.

I don’t need everyone to be like me. I look for the basics: say hello, keep the path clear, respect quiet hours, pitch in when something needs doing. If you’re new and you show up to spread mulch or help fix the busted fence, you’re already halfway to being “ours.” I’ve learned more about people over swapped tomatoes and borrowed ladders than from any debate.

I’ll admit, sometimes I feel awkward at first. I grew up where most folks had similar stories, so when I can’t find the right words or customs are different, I fall back on simple courtesies—offer a hand, share extra zucchini, ask a name twice if I miss it. Nine times out of ten, that breaks the ice. What makes me uneasy isn’t difference; it’s disrespect—trash left behind, music blasting at midnight, cars blocking driveways, or a vibe that says, “your rules don’t apply to me.” That’s not about where you’re from; that’s about being a good neighbor.

When people show they care—watch a kid for five minutes, check on the older guy after a storm, bring a dish to the potluck—that’s when the garden feels like a little town square. We don’t have to agree on everything. If we can share the work and look out for each other, I’m comfortable. That’s belonging, right there.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
J: For me, the way to make everybody comfortable is to keep it simple and consistent: we judge by behavior, not by labels. One set of expectations in shared spaces—clean up after yourself, keep noise reasonable, be safe around kids, and treat people with basic respect. If we stick to those basics, most differences don’t turn into problems.

On tough stuff like alcoholism or substance use, I lean toward firm kindness. The garden and common areas should be safe and calm—no intoxication in the space, no paraphernalia left where kids could find it. If someone’s struggling, we offer a hand—point to local support, check in if they look unwell—but we don’t enable, and we don’t let safety slide. If a situation gets risky, you call for help and you don’t feel bad about it. Everyone’s dignity matters, including the neighbors who need a peaceful place to be.

With infectious diseases, I think privacy and good hygiene come first. We don’t pry into people’s health or spread rumors. We keep shared tools clean, have handwashing stations at events, and follow public health guidance if something specific comes up. If someone asks for a bit more space or a small change to feel safe, we try to accommodate without making them feel singled out. Respect goes a long way.

Different racial, religious, and language backgrounds—this is where patience and curiosity help. Learn names, ask once more if you missed it, and don’t be shy about using a translation app or pointing to a sign. Post the garden rules in plain language, maybe with pictures. If someone’s observant of certain customs, we respect that—no big speeches, just everyday courtesy. Shared work builds bridges faster than any lecture.

Sexual orientation or how folks structure their family—honestly, that’s their business. Hold everyone to the same neighbor standards and keep moral judging out of it. If two guys bring a casserole to the potluck or an unmarried couple shows up to fix the gate, they’re part of the solution. You treat them the same as anyone else: thank them, hand them a wrench, pass the lemonade.

Where do we need more communication and tolerance? A few places:
- Language barriers: slow down, point, smile. Pair folks up so someone who’s been around can walk a newcomer through the routines.
- Noise, parties, and smoking: set clear hours and boundaries, write them down, and remind gently before it becomes a complaint. Most people will meet you halfway if they know the expectations.
- Safety around kids and tools: quick reminders and posted notes help—store sharp tools, keep glass out, no open containers if that’s the rule.
- Health concerns: let people say what they need without grilling them; “Is there anything we can do to make this comfortable for you?” is enough.

Why I feel this way is pretty simple. Fairness means nobody gets special treatment, and nobody gets singled out for who they are. Belonging is earned by showing up and respecting the shared space. Community is strongest when we mix compassion with boundaries—lend a hand, but keep the place safe. If we keep the rules clear, apply them evenly, and lead with small kindnesses—names learned, chairs shared, tools put back—folks relax. And once people relax, they talk. When they talk, they start to trust. That’s the foundation that lets a diverse block feel like home.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character06_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
J: When jobs are tight, fairness starts with reciprocity: the people who’ve been paying into the pot—taxes, time, Little League coaching—shouldn’t feel pushed to the back of the line. At the same time, I don’t blame the guy who crossed a continent to feed his kids. The real problem is when the rules are fuzzy or not enforced, and employers use that to undercut wages. So I aim for “clear rules, same rules,” and make sure work goes to whoever meets the standard at a fair wage.

How I’d balance locals and migrant workers:

- Local-first, with honest exceptions: If there are qualified local residents or long-time legal residents ready to work at the posted wage, they get first crack. If a job’s sitting open—nurses on night shift, harvest crews, welders with specific certs—then bring in folks to fill the gap. Don’t pretend there’s a shortage if the real issue is a rock-bottom wage.

- Wage floors and enforcement: Make it illegal to pay anyone less than the going rate for that job in that area—locals and migrants alike. Set the visa wage above the prevailing wage so it can’t be used to drive pay down. Crack down on off‑the‑books hiring and misclassification. Big fines for companies playing games, and protect whistleblowers so workers aren’t scared to report abuse.

- Invest in our own people: If employers say they can’t find workers, require them to help train them—apprenticeships, community college vouchers, paid traineeships. Prioritize young folks, veterans, and laid‑off workers for these slots. If you want a permit to hire from abroad, show receipts that you’ve posted jobs widely and funded training locally.

- Demand‑driven visas with real review: Allow visas tied to verified shortages, with sunset dates and yearly audits. If the shortage eases, you dial the numbers back. If it persists, you keep it steady. No “set it and forget it.”

- Seasonal and essential work with dignity: Agriculture, elder care, construction—if we need extra hands in peak seasons, set up clean, temporary pathways. Give workers decent housing standards, the right to switch employers, and a guaranteed ticket home and back next season if they want. That reduces abuse and churn.

- Community impact support: When new workers arrive, the strain shows up in schools, clinics, and housing. A small fee on certain work visas could flow straight back to the towns absorbing the growth—ESL classes, bus routes, building inspectors—so locals don’t feel like they’re carrying it alone.

- Humanitarian lane, backed by resources: Refugees and people fleeing danger shouldn’t be lumped into a jobs debate. If we take them in, fund the resettlement properly so they can stand on their own feet—language, job placement, counseling—and so host communities have support too.

- One standard on the job: Safety rules, overtime, taxes—same for everyone. Unions or worker councils should be open to all workers in a shop, so no one’s used as a wedge to break standards.

- Tighten the gray areas: Use simple work-eligibility checks, and put the heat on repeat‑offender employers, not just the worker at the bottom. If the rules are real and consistent, the “race to the bottom” slows down.

Why I land here is personal. I’ve watched buddies get undercut by cash-only crews and I’ve also worked alongside immigrants who outworked all of us and kept a job site alive. The villain, most days, isn’t the worker—it’s a system that rewards cutting corners. Fairness, to me, means:
- People who’ve carried the load get a fair shot first.
- Nobody’s wages get shaved because someone is easier to exploit.
- We fill real gaps so businesses don’t fold and shelves don’t go empty.
- We treat everyone who’s doing the work with basic respect and the same rulebook.

That’s not “open the floodgates,” and it’s not “slam the door.” It’s a middle lane where we protect standards, grow the pie where we can, and keep the social fabric from tearing when times are lean.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character06_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
J: I see a little truth in most of those arguments. The trick is scale and guardrails—what we allow, how fast, and under what rules.

- Filling vital roles: Makes sense to me. I’ve seen hospitals short on aides, farms scrambling for pickers, shops begging for welders. If jobs are posted at a fair wage and still sit empty, bringing in workers is reasonable. But if “shortage” is code for “we don’t want to pay,” that’s on employers, not on the labor pool.

- Cultural diversity and vitality: I like the energy—new food, new music, different ways of doing things. It can wake up a sleepy town. It works best when there’s a shared floor of norms—respect for laws, learning English over time, showing up for the community. Diversity plus shared expectations feels good; diversity with everyone in their own silo can breed friction.

- Security concerns: Wanting secure borders and decent vetting is common sense. Most immigrants I’ve worked with are law‑abiding and cautious—they’ve got too much to lose. Big terror scares tied to newcomers are rare, and we already vet refugees hard. Still, we should:
  - Focus on violent offenders and trafficking rings.
  - Track visa overstays better.
  - Put heat on employers who build shadow economies.
  That targets real risks without painting everyone as a threat.

- Humanitarian perspective: I believe in giving people fleeing war or persecution a shot. But if we say yes, we owe them and the host towns real support—language classes, job placement, trauma counseling—and some help for schools and clinics taking on the load. If we don’t back it up, we hurt them and we sour locals.

- Jobs and wages fears: This one hits close. On average, studies say the overall economy can grow and most wages aren’t wrecked. But averages hide pockets of pain. Folks like me, without a fancy degree, can feel the pressure in certain trades or towns. I think:
  - Short‑term, local impacts can be real; long‑term, the pie can grow.
  - Wage floors, apprenticeship pipelines, and enforcing the same rules for everyone keep things fair.
  - Visa numbers should flex with unemployment and verified shortages.

- Social tension: When change is fast, even good change can feel like loss. Schools, housing, and streets don’t stretch overnight. If we pace growth and fund the basics—ESL teachers, bus routes, building inspectors—tempers cool and people have time to adjust.

What seems reasonable:
- Fill real labor gaps at fair wages, not as a workaround to cheapen pay.
- Strong borders and clean, transparent legal channels.
- Equal standards on the job—safety, taxes, overtime—for all workers.
- Properly funded refugee resettlement and community support.
- Expectation of integration over time—English, civics, respect for local laws.

What needs more facts or honest dialogue:
- Claims of “immigrants drive crime.” My understanding is crime rates among immigrants are generally lower, but let’s look at local data, not headlines.
- “They’re taking all the jobs.” Which jobs, at what wages, and were they posted and trained for? Show the numbers.
- “They’re a drain on welfare.” It varies by program and timeframe. We should look at lifetime contributions versus costs, and the second generation too.
- “They don’t assimilate.” Some places do a great job building bridges; others don’t. Let’s measure English acquisition, workforce participation, and civic involvement instead of going by vibe.

How to move the conversation:
- Use local dashboards: job vacancies, wage trends, school enrollment, housing supply.
- Put employers, unions, cops, teachers, churches, and immigrant groups at the same table. The people living it day to day are better guides than national TV.
- Build in feedback loops—if a policy is straining a town, adjust the throttle; if shortages persist, keep the gate open with guardrails.

Bottom line, I’m for a door with a lock and a doorbell: clear rules, fair enforcement, and a welcome for those who come in the right way and pull their weight. That respects both the folks already here and the ones willing to join the team.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character06_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
J: I’m not for flinging the doors wide, and I’m not for slamming them shut. I’d take a middle road: admit people based on verified job demand, set numeric limits that flex with conditions, and keep a separate, well‑funded humanitarian lane. The aim is clear rules, steady pacing, and equal standards so wages and neighborhoods don’t get whipsawed.

What I’d support:
- Demand‑driven worker visas, with caps by sector: Tie numbers to real shortages shown by posted jobs, wage offers, and training attempts. Review yearly; dial up or down based on unemployment and vacancy data.
- Wage floors and portability: Set visa wages above the local prevailing rate, and let workers change employers so no one’s trapped or used to undercut pay.
- Seasonal/essential pathways: Agriculture, elder care, construction in peak seasons—clean temporary programs with decent housing standards and a return option, so employers and towns can plan.
- National cap that flexes: A baseline number that adjusts with the economy and local capacity—schools, clinics, housing. No “open the spigot and hope.”
- Family reunification, paced and close‑kin: Prioritize spouses and minor kids, with sponsorship so folks don’t sink under the load. Keep it predictable, not a backdoor.
- Humanitarian/refugee lane, funded properly: If we take people fleeing danger, back it up—ESL, job placement, counseling—and send support to the communities hosting them.
- Local impact support: A small visa fee flowing to towns absorbing the growth—ESL teachers, bus routes, building inspectors—so locals see the benefit, not just the strain.
- Employer accountability: Simple work‑eligibility checks, big penalties for repeat abusers, protect whistleblowers. Put the heat on the folks gaming the system, not just the guy on the ladder.
- Earned stability: For those who work, pay taxes, learn English, and keep a clean record over several years, offer a path to permanent status. That rewards contribution and encourages integration.

Why this mix:
- Fairness: Locals and long‑time legal residents get a fair shot first. Nobody’s wage is shaved because someone is easier to exploit.
- Predictability: Caps and audits stop sudden surges that overwhelm schools or housing, and they prevent employers from crying “shortage” when it’s just low pay.
- Integration: English, civics, and community standards matter. People should join the team, not just the payroll.
- Humanity without chaos: We can help the persecuted, but we owe them and host towns real support so everyone can stand on their feet.

Complete openness ignores capacity and undercuts trust. A blanket refusal hurts farms, hospitals, and small businesses that genuinely can’t fill slots. The balanced policy is a door with a lock and a doorbell: you ring, we check, we welcome you if you meet the standard—and everyone inside plays by the same rulebook. That’s how you keep wages fair, neighborhoods steady, and the country’s heart open without losing its footing.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character06_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character06_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:

For my own views, I came out a little more disciplined and a little more generous at the same time. More disciplined about wage floors, enforcement, and tying worker visas to real shortages with a feedback loop. More generous about a properly funded humanitarian lane and the idea that belonging is earned through everyday contribution, not pedigree. And I’m more convinced that if we send resources to the towns doing the absorbing—and keep one rulebook for everyone—most tensions ease.

I also realized how much he trusted small, concrete habits over big speeches: post the rules plainly, apply them evenly, learn names, fix what’s broken. That’s changed how I think about policy—less about slogans, more about nuts and bolts and local dashboards. In that way, talking as him didn’t just bring him back; it sharpened my own compass.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character06_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?

I think it’s important we don’t just stick to our own kind—otherwise, what’s the point of community? But I’d be lying if I said it was always easy. Sometimes I wish people made more effort to join in, learn about local traditions, and maybe meet us halfway.

So, I’m open to getting to know folks, but I do appreciate when there’s some common ground. The neighborhood’s changing, and I’m trying to keep up—just hope that everyone, old-timers and new arrivals, can find ways to connect, respect each other, and build something together.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character06_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough one, and I’ve thought about it a lot. When there aren’t enough jobs to go around, I think fairness means looking out for the folks who’ve been here and paid in, first. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character06_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Looking at it from a national level, I see why people have strong opinions on all sides. Some of these arguments make sense to me, and some I think get blown out of proportion or aren’t talked about honestly enough.

First, I get the point that immigrants fill jobs Americans don’t always want—like working on farms, in kitchens, or doing tough manual labor. I’ve seen it myself, and I can’t argue with the fact that certain industries might collapse without them. That’s a reasonable point, and I respect people who work hard, no matter where they come from.

And I’ll admit, having different cultures and backgrounds does make a place more interesting—new food, music, ideas. It can be good for the country, as long as people still make an effort to become part of the bigger community, not just stick in their own group.

But I also think the concerns about jobs and wages are very real, especially for people like me who worked blue-collar jobs most of their life. When there’s more competition for work, pay goes down and people get pushed out. I know folks who lost their jobs or had to settle for less because companies hired cheaper labor. That’s not just a feeling—it’s something you can see in certain towns and industries.

Security is tougher to talk about. Some people go too far, blaming immigrants for all the crime or for terrorism. That’s not fair, and most immigrants are here to work and live in peace. Still, if there are problems—like gangs or crime linked to certain groups—then it’s something that should be looked at honestly, not just swept under the rug or blown out of proportion. We need real facts, not just rumors or politics.

As for humanitarian reasons, I do believe America should help people fleeing war, violence, or poverty. That’s part of what makes us who we are. But I think there has to be limits and checks—make sure people are really in need, and make sure the system isn’t being abused.

So, which are reasonable? The arguments about jobs, wages, and integration are real and need to be discussed openly. The role immigrants play in the economy—true, but it needs balance. Cultural diversity is good, but it works best if people actually join in and contribute. Security concerns need facts and not just fearmongering. And humanitarian help is important, but it shouldn’t mean ignoring the needs of people who already live here.

A lot of these debates need more honest dialogue and real data. Too often, people just repeat what they hear on the news or from politicians. We need to talk more, listen to what’s really happening, and be willing to adjust our views if the facts say differently. That’s what I always wanted: more common sense, less yelling.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character06_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I’m honest, I don’t think complete openness is realistic or fair—not to the people already living here, and not even to the newcomers. You have to have some way of keeping things in balance, or else you end up with more problems than solutions.

So, the approach that makes the most sense to me is a mix: mainly admitting people based on job demand, but also setting some numerical limits depending on what the country can handle at the time. If there’s a real shortage in certain industries—like agriculture, healthcare, construction—then it makes sense to let people in to fill those gaps. But if jobs are scarce for everyone, you can’t just keep bringing folks in, or you hurt working people who are already struggling.

Numerical limits help keep things fair. You can’t let in more people than the schools, hospitals, and communities can support. It’s not about being mean—it’s about making sure everyone who’s here gets a fair shot and a decent life. Maybe some years the numbers go up, maybe some years they go down. The government ought to listen to local communities about what’s working and what’s not.

I also think it’s important to have special provisions for refugees or people in real danger. We should help those who need it most, but still keep checks in place so the system isn’t abused.

The idea of refusing entry altogether just doesn’t sit right with me—it’s too harsh and doesn’t reflect what this country is supposed to be about. But at the same time, just letting everyone in doesn’t work, either.

What matters for fairness and social integration is making sure newcomers have a way to become part of the community—learn English, understand local customs, and contribute like anyone else. I’d like to see more programs that help people settle in and mix with their neighbors, not just live on the margins.

So, my policy choice would be: let people in where there’s real need for workers, keep sensible limits, and put some effort into helping people really become part of the country. That’s the kind of balance I’d want to see.

*gestures emphatically*

What frustrates me is when I see companies bringing in foreign workers on special visas when there are plenty of local folks who could do those jobs with a bit of training. Or when businesses hire undocumented workers because they can pay them less and skip out on benefits. That's not fair to anybody - not to the local workers who lose opportunities, and not to the migrants who get exploited.

*sighs*

I think a balanced approach would be something like: First, invest in training programs for local residents who've been displaced by economic changes. Give them first crack at retooling for new industries. Second, have a clear, enforceable immigration policy that allows for legal migration based on actual labor needs - not just what's cheapest for big corporations.

And third - this is important - hold employers accountable. The problem isn't the guy coming across the border looking for work to feed his family. It's the companies knowingly hiring undocumented workers to boost their profit margins.

Bottom line is, we need policies that recognize both the contributions and needs of established community members while still allowing reasonable, controlled immigration that fills genuine gaps in our workforce. That's the kind of fairness I can get behind.

*expression grows more serious*

Most immigrants are law-abiding - probably more so than average because they don't want trouble. But proper vetting makes sense. We need to know who's coming in. That's just common sense.

The humanitarian angle - helping refugees fleeing persecution - that's part of what America stands for. I'm proud of that tradition. But we need sustainable numbers and proper resources to help people integrate successfully. Otherwise, we're not really helping anyone in the long run.

*leans forward*

*shakes head slightly*

*sighs*

Bottom line - I think reasonable people can see valid points on multiple sides here. The problem is we've gotten so polarized that acknowledging complexity gets you attacked from both extremes. Job demand should definitely be a major consideration - bringing in people with skills we actually need. The healthcare sector, certain types of manufacturing, agriculture - these areas have genuine shortages. But I'd want to see requirements that employers prove they've made real efforts to hire and train American workers first.

*nods firmly*

Family reunification should remain part of the equation, but maybe more focused on immediate family - spouses, minor children. The chain migration that can bring in distant relatives without regard to skills or our economic needs doesn't make sense to me.

I'd also support a moderate refugee program. America should remain a beacon for people fleeing genuine persecution. But we need proper vetting and resources to help them integrate.

*leans forward*

Now, for the integration piece - this is crucial. I'd support requiring basic English proficiency within a reasonable timeframe, maybe with exceptions for elderly folks. I'd like to see civics education as part of the immigration process - understanding American history, values, and how our system works.

Legal status should come with both rights and responsibilities clearly spelled out. Pay taxes, obey laws, participate in your community. In return, you get protection under our laws and access to services you help fund.

*expression softens slightly*

For those already here illegally, I'm not for mass deportations - that's impractical and would tear apart communities. But I don't support blanket amnesty either. Maybe a path to legal status - not necessarily citizenship - with penalties, background checks, and requirements to learn English and civics.

The fairest policy, to my mind, is one that's clear, consistently enforced, and balanced between our traditions of welcoming immigrants and our need to maintain social cohesion and economic opportunity for all. No one gets everything they want, but everyone understands the rules and can see they're being applied equally.

*shakes head slightly*

What's unfair is what we have now - confusion, selective enforcement, and policies that swing wildly depending on who's in office. Nobody benefits from that chaos except maybe politicians looking for campaign issues and businesses exploiting cheap labor.

But sometimes it feels like we’re so busy celebrating how different everyone is that we forget to celebrate what we have in common—the garden, the sidewalks, the school zone, the quiet at night. That’s what community is. Not just bodies in houses. It’s shared effort.

And look—some folks struggle. I get that. I’ve struggled. But struggle don’t excuse disrespect. And integration don’t mean losing who you are—but it does mean adopting some of who *we* are. Speak English in public. Follow the laws. Teach your kids to do the same.

That’s how you belong. Not because someone hands it to you. Because you earn it—right alongside the rest of us.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*Leans back a little, pulls a blade of grass, rolls it between his fingers.*

Look… I ain’t the kind to judge folks for their private lives. What two people do in their own home—that’s on them. If two men want to live together, raise kids, keep a dog and mow the lawn every Saturday—fine by me, long as they’re not shoving it in my face or expecting me to call it something it ain’t. Same goes for unmarried couples. People don’t get married like they used to. I don’t have to like it, but I see it. Life changes.

But here’s where I draw the line: when “tolerance” starts meaning *silence*. When I can’t say something’s wrong without being called a bigot.

Take alcoholism. My uncle was one. Drank himself to death at 62. Wasn’t pretty. Missed birthdays. Broke promises. We loved him, but we didn’t excuse him. And nobody told us we had to “understand” it like it was just another lifestyle choice. It was a sickness—one he kept feeding.

Same with drugs. I’ve seen what opioids did to this town. Lost jobs. Kids taken by CPS. Houses boarded up. Now, some of these folks coming in from other countries? They don’t bring that. In fact, a lot of ’em seem more straight-laced than our own kids. That I respect.

But then you’ve got public health—HIV, hepatitis, TB—things that spread. I remember when the clinic opened that needle exchange downtown. I asked, “Who’s making sure these folks aren’t putting the rest of us at risk?” Nobody answered. Just said, “It’s harm reduction.” Well, whose harm? The user’s? Or mine, when I’m walking through the park and find dirty needles near the swings?

So yeah, compassion matters. But so does accountability.

Communication? Sure, we need more of it—but both ways. Not just “you must accept this,” but “here’s what we expect if you want to live safely and peacefully together.” Like language. If you’re here, learn English. Not tomorrow, not in ten years—start *now*. Because how am I supposed to talk to you about the water main break if you don’t understand the notice on the door?

And diseases? If you’re sick, get treated. Don’t wait till it spreads. That’s not intolerance—that’s common sense.

I’ll treat anyone with dignity, no matter their race, religion, or who they love. But dignity goes both ways. You want to feel comfortable here? Then show some respect for the place and the people already in it. Don’t expect us to erase our way of life so you can stay in yours untouched.

Tolerance shouldn’t mean losing your backbone.

I think what makes *everyone* feel comfortable is clear expectations—not a free-for-all where anything goes as long as it’s labeled “diversity.” We can be decent without being naive. We can help without enabling.

That’s what my dad taught me: help the man who wants to stand up. Don’t carry the one who just wants to lie down and blame the world.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character06_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*Crosses arms, looks down at the cracked leather of his work boots before speaking slow and even.*

Fairness? When jobs are thin and folks back home are struggling—fairness means *we come first.* Plain as that.

I’m not saying kick nobody in. But don’t bring in people from other countries to fill jobs while our own veterans are sleeping in trailers, while high school grads can’t find a shift at the warehouse, while men my age—who’ve been here their whole lives—get told they’re “overqualified” or “too old to train.”

You want fairness? Hire local first. Train local first. Pay a wage that covers rent and groceries—not some penny-an-hour gig with no benefits, just because you can import workers who’ll take it and won’t complain.

I saw it happen at the packing plant. Ten years ago, they started bringing in guest workers—H-2B visas, they called it. Said there was “a labor shortage.” A shortage? I knew three guys laid off from that same plant the year before! One drives Uber now. One’s on disability for his back—probably never should’ve left that job in the first place.

But these new guys? They live ten to a house, send most of their pay home, don’t ask questions. Good for the boss. Bad for us.

So when someone says, “They do jobs Americans won’t do,” I bristle. That’s a lie. Americans *will* do any job—if it pays enough to survive. The truth is, Americans won’t do slave wages. There’s a difference.

Fairness means if a job’s important—if it keeps food on tables, roads plowed, hospitals running—then it deserves fair pay, fair hours, fair treatment. And if it does, then locals will take it. No need to go halfway across the world to find warm bodies.

And let’s talk about timing. When times are hard—when the factory closes, when inflation eats your paycheck—that’s when people feel the squeeze most. That’s when resentment builds. Not because we hate outsiders. But because we see doors closing for us while new ones open for folks who just got here.

So balance? Yeah, there’s gotta be balance. Let in workers if there’s *real* need—but only after proving no qualified local can do the job. And make sure those jobs pay union-scale or close to it. No undercutting. No exploiting temporary status so they can’t speak up.

And while we’re at it—how about investing in *our* people? Retraining programs. Apprenticeships. Help for older workers. Not just shrug and say, “Sorry, the market changed.”

Because this ain’t just economics. It’s dignity. My neighbor Dave—he was in manufacturing 28 years. Plant moved to Mexico, then started hiring guest workers for the few jobs left. He applied. Got turned down. They hired two guys from Honduras instead. Same skill set. But they’d accept half the pay.

How’s that fair?

I’m not against immigration. I’m against using it to break the working class—both newcomers *and* locals. Pit us against each other so the bosses can keep wages low and power high.

That’s what I call rigged.

So yeah—let people come. But not over our heads. Not on our backs. There’s room for everyone—but not at the expense of those already here, already struggling, already loyal to this place.

Fairness means you don’t replace us to accommodate others. You lift us *together*.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character06_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*Leans forward, elbows on knees, voice lower now—measured, like he’s weighing each word before it leaves.*

Alright. Let’s lay it out like I see it.

First—the labor argument. Yeah, immigrants *do* fill jobs. Farm work, meatpacking, construction, some of the nursing homes… people come in and do hard work, often for less than locals want to take. That part’s true. And if those spots stay empty, things break down. Crops rot. Houses don’t get built. So from a practical standpoint, that side’s got merit.

But—and this is a big *but*—that doesn’t mean we just open the door and say “come on in.” Because when you let in too many, too fast, without planning, what happens? Wages go down. Employers start preferring newcomers because they’re easier to control—less likely to complain, less connected, sometimes not even speaking the language. So the American worker—the guy with student loans, a mortgage, a kid starting college—he gets squeezed out. Not because he’s lazy. Because the system’s rigged against him.

So I’ll accept “labor shortage” as real—*if* it’s proven. Show me the numbers. Prove nobody local applied. Prove the wage offered was fair. Otherwise, it’s just a cover for cheap labor. And that ain’t fairness. That’s exploitation wearing a nice suit.

Now, cultural diversity. Look, I’ve eaten Ethiopian food. Been to a Diwali festival once with my niece. Nice music. Good food. I’m not scared of different cultures. But let’s not pretend diversity is always smooth. You drop folks from completely different worlds into a small town with its own way of life—different values, different religions, different views on women, on family, on law—and yeah, tensions rise. Not because people are hateful. Because change *hurts* when it’s forced and fast.

I saw it in the school board meetings when they tried to change the curriculum—suddenly, things were being taught that didn’t line up with how most of us raised our kids. And instead of talking, they called us backward. That shuts down conversation.

So diversity can bring vitality—but only if there’s integration. Not assimilation overnight, but a two-way street. You bring your strengths. We keep ours. And we meet somewhere in the middle. Without that? You end up with parallel societies—same city, different rules. That’s not strength. That’s a time bomb.

Security? I don’t like saying it, but I’d be foolish to ignore it. After 9/11, we woke up. Then Boston. Then smaller attacks since. Most immigrants aren’t terrorists—that I know. But it only takes one. And if border screening’s sloppy, or asylum claims are abused, or vetting’s weak because we’re in a hurry to look compassionate… then we’re playing with fire.

Humanitarian angle—I’ll give you that. Refugees fleeing war, dictatorship, starvation? That tugs at me. My granddad came after WWII—displaced person camp in Germany. We took him in. Gave him a chance. He worked three jobs, learned English, never took welfare. That’s the kind of story I respect.

But today? It’s different scale. Different pace. And I ask: Are we helping them become *part of us*—or just warehousing them in housing projects, handing out checks, letting them live in their old world while ignoring ours?

And what about our own poor? Our own veterans sleeping under bridges? Where’s the compassion for them?

So yes—help those in real need. But do it smart. Do it slowly. Make sure we have room—not just beds, but schools, clinics, jobs. Not add to the strain on folks already barely holding on.

As for crime… I’ve read the studies. Some say immigrants commit *less* crime than native-born. Maybe so. But I’ve also seen neighborhoods change—once safe, now you think twice about walking at night. Is it the immigrants? Sometimes. Sometimes it’s the chaos of transition. No cohesion. No trust. When people don’t know each other, don’t share values, don’t speak the same language—crime fills the gap.

So I won’t say “all immigrants are criminals”—that’s stupid. But I won’t pretend open borders are risk-free. There’s got to be order. Vetting. Consequences.

At the end of the day, I believe most people want to do right. Newcomers included. But systems matter. Intentions don’t feed families.

The viewpoints I find reasonable? The ones rooted in balance. In evidence. In honesty about trade-offs.

The ones that need more proof? The ones that say, “Trust us, it’ll all work out.” Or “If you question anything, you’re a hater.” That shuts down thinking.

We need dialogue—not slogans. Facts—not fear. And above all, we need to remember that a nation isn’t just land and laws. It’s shared belief. Shared sacrifice. A common thread.

Lose that, and it doesn’t matter how diverse or rich or “compassionate” we are—we’ll fall apart from the inside.

And I’m not ready to watch that happen. Not on my watch.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character06_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*Stands slowly, brushes dirt off his pants, looks out across the garden like he’s sizing up a job that needs doing.*

Alright. Let’s cut the noise.

Complete openness? No. That’s not generosity—that’s surrender. A country without borders isn’t a country. It’s chaos with zoning laws. You can’t just say “come on in” and expect communities—especially working-class ones like mine—to absorb everyone without breaking. Schools fill. Clinics overflow. Wages drop. Trust erodes. I won’t pretend that doesn’t happen.

Refusing *all* foreign workers? Also no. Stubborn. Unrealistic. Some jobs need doing, and if we’re honest, some Americans won’t take them—at least, not at the wages employers want to pay. But again—that’s not the immigrant’s fault. That’s a broken labor system.

So where’s the middle?

I’d go with this: **admit people based on real job demand, with strict numerical limits, and a clear path to integration—not just work permits that trap people in one job for years.**

Let me break it down.

First—**job-based entry**, but only after proving no qualified local was available. Not “we couldn’t find anyone who’d work for $12 an hour.” I mean, *tried to hire at fair wage*, advertised locally, trained if needed. If still empty? Then bring someone in. But tie that visa to the job, yes—but also give the worker rights. Can’t be scared to report abuse. Can’t be held hostage by their employer.

Second—**numerical limits**, set every year by Congress, based on actual economic capacity. Not pulled from thin air. Not emotional appeals. Look at housing, schools, infrastructure. How many can this town, this city, this region *actually* handle without buckling? Respect that limit. Enforce it.

Third—**integration requirements.** Not optional. When you come here legally, you commit. Learn English within five years—classes provided, but attendance required. Pass a civics test. Know the Constitution, the holidays, the laws. Understand what being American *means* beyond a paycheck.

And family reunification? Fine—after five years, once established, tax-paying, clean record. Not immediate chain migration where one person brings in ten relatives who all depend on aid.

As for refugees—small, vetted numbers. Real threats, real documentation. Security checks that *mean* something. Not backlog asylum claims for years while people live in limbo, feeding off social services we can’t afford.

And—this is key—**no automatic citizenship.** Earn it. Ten years minimum. Work history. Language. No serious crimes. Contribute before you claim full membership.

Fairness? It means locals aren’t last in line. It means hardworking immigrants aren’t exploited. It means communities aren’t overwhelmed.

Social integration? That doesn’t happen by accident. It takes time, effort, and expectations. You don’t build unity by ignoring differences—you build it by asking everyone to meet in the middle.

So yeah, controlled, orderly, *fair* immigration—I can live with that.

But open door? Or closed fist? Neither works for people like me. For folks in towns like ours.

We don’t want handouts. We don’t want to hate. We just want a system that treats us like we matter—that remembers the people already here, already struggling, already loyal.

A good policy doesn’t choose between compassion and common sense. It finds a way to have both.

And if it can’t? Then it’s not a policy. It’s politics. And politics don’t feed families.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character06_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character06_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*Pauses. Takes off his cap, runs a hand through thinning hair, then looks down for a long moment before speaking—softer now, more reflective.*

You know… I thought I knew where he stood. I mean, we talked plenty over the years—beer on the porch, union meetings, arguments at the VFW hall. But stepping into his voice like this… it wasn’t just repeating old lines. It brought him *back*. Not the caricature people might’ve made of him—the “angry white guy,” the “left behind”—but the real man. The one who worried about fairness not because he feared change, but because he’d spent his life playing by the rules and watching others cut corners while he struggled.

What surprised me? How much grief is underneath it all.

It’s not really about immigration, not at the core. It’s about loss. Loss of dignity. Loss of place. He saw his dad retire from the same job he started at 19. Saw the union protect them. Saw neighbors help each other without being asked. Now? Jobs come and go. Loyalty means nothing. Towns change so fast you don’t recognize your own street. And when you speak up, they call you bitter. Or racist. Even if all you’re saying is, *“Don’t forget us.”*

Embodying him today… it reminded me that his views weren’t born in hate. They were born in fear—fear of being erased. Of working hard and still losing ground. Of raising kids in a world where effort doesn’t guarantee anything anymore.

And that made me question my own assumptions.

I used to think, “Just open the door. More people, more ideas, more energy.” Simpler that way. Noble, even. But sitting here as him… I had to face the cost. Not just economic—but emotional. Social. What happens to community when trust frays? When people stop believing in shared rules?

So no, I wouldn’t say I’ve changed sides. But I understand the weight of the burden differently now.

He wasn’t against newcomers. He was against *unmanaged* change. Against a system that helps everyone *except* the working stiff who’s been here all along.

And maybe… maybe that’s where we’ve failed each other. We let it become “us vs. them”—immigrant vs. native, city vs. town, young vs. old—instead of asking: *How do we build something that works for all of us?*

Character06_M didn’t want to shut the world out. He just wanted to know his place was still there when he came home.

And maybe—just maybe—that’s not too much to ask.

So thank you. For bringing him back. Not to argue. Not to judge. But to listen.

Because some truths don’t shout. They just sit quietly in a garden, pulling weeds, wondering if anyone remembers what belonging used to feel like.
